newsitem.title: FRANCE: France launching historic military cuts in Africa.
newsitem.headline: France launching historic military cuts in Africa.

text.p: France is poised for a historic reduction of military forces in Africa, a continent where Paris has clung to a faded aura as a colonial superpower.

Defence Minister Alain Richard was leaving Paris on Tuesday afternoon at the start of a three-day trip to Gabon, Chad and the Central African Republic, to start outlining cuts despite French fears of opening the door to wider U.S. influence.
"The end of an epoch", the conservative daily Le Figaro said in a front-page editorial.
France is cutting back in Africa under pressure for budget cuts and amid belated realisation that Africa needs less policing after the end of the Cold War.
"Forty years after decolonisation, Paris wants, in effect, to redefine all its relations with the black continent," it said.

New Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's government plans to cut the number of French troops by about 40 percent to 5,000 from 8,350, government sources said, extending a planned reduction by the previous centre-right government.

The biggest cut will be closure of the French garrisons in Central African Republic, one of six nations where troops are based, the daily Liberation said. It said Richard would announce the decision to President Ange-Felix Patasse.

The cuts mark a watershed for a nation that has often intervened to prop up or topple African strongmen. The end of the Cold War has also devalued the anti-communist credentials of surviving French-backed dinosaurs.
Pierre Messmer, defence minister to General Charles de Gaulle, said he was satisfied with plans to cut back, saying it was something he had favoured for 20 years. But he warned of pitfalls ahead.
"If we cut back...we must be able to transport the necessary military means from mainland France if we want to intervene, as happens from time to time."

"And I would point out that we don't have these means, especially in the air," he told Europe 1 radio. France has launched an overhaul of the armed forces, including a shift to a smaller, all-professional force.
Paris has suffered a string of setbacks in Africa, culminating in the overthrow of long-term ally president Mobutu Sese Seko this year in what was Zaire by Laurent Kabila's forces.

Before a left-wing victory in France's June 1 election, Jospin said the former government's support for Mobutu sealed "the bankruptcy of France's Africa policy" under conservative President Jacques Chirac.
Yet French leaders from both left and right share blame.

France's Africa policy suffered a jolt under late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand with the fall of a Hutu-led government in Rwanda in 1994, driven out by Ugandan-backed Tutsi rebels after genocide blamed on Hutu extremists.
Many of the Hutu militiamen fled to Zaire amid a flood of refugees, protected by French troops sent on a relief mission meant to help shield the innocent.
Messmer said Mitterrand gave some "extremely unfortunate" examples of interference in Africa, especially in Rwanda.

And Mobutu, now apparently unwelcome in France, is undergoing cancer treatment in a Moroccan hospital, far from a pink villa on the French Riviera where he resided for long periods under both Mitterrand and Chirac.

Messmer dismissed fears that cuts in Africa would mean abdicating in favour of Washington. He said the United States had shown little interest in helping Liberia, a one-time protectorate, when it descended into anarchy.
"The Americans operate with the idea of 'trade not aid'. Africans agree with trading but they also like aid," Messmer said. "Under these conditions, Europe retains a certain charm for most Africans."
